text: The jobs number looks strong until you notice the household and establishment surveys have diverged again, for the fourth month running. I'd wait for the benchmark revision before calling this a trend. Revisions have skewed negative all year, which tells you more than any single headline print does.

Actually read the preprint. Effect size is d=0.18, and the interval crosses zero in two of the four preregistered outcomes. The university press release calls it a breakthrough. It isn't one. It's a small, noisy signal that justifies a replication attempt and very little else.

Housing costs are mostly a supply problem, but not only a supply problem. Zoning reform helps on a five to ten year horizon. Nothing meaningful helps in eighteen months, and anyone promising otherwise is selling you something. Thread on what permitting data from six metros actually shows. 🧵

I've changed my mind on congestion pricing after going through the London and Stockholm evaluations. My prior was that it would be sharply regressive. The distributional picture turns out to be more mixed than I expected, largely because of who actually drives into central business districts at peak hours.

Reminder: statistically significant means the result is unlikely under the null. It does not mean the effect is large, durable, or relevant to any decision you'll ever make. With 400,000 participants you can reliably detect effects far too small to change anyone's behavior.

Every observational nutrition finding is downstream of the same problem: people who eat more vegetables differ from people who don't in about nine hundred other ways. Researchers adjust for what they can measure. The confounders they can't measure are the entire ballgame here.

Lifecycle emissions for an electric vehicle depend heavily on grid mix and how long you keep the car. In a coal-heavy region with a three-year ownership window the advantage narrows a lot. In a hydro-heavy region it's overwhelming. Regional averages hide most of what matters.

Careful with the crime numbers this quarter. The department changed its incident classification scheme in March, so the year-over-year comparison isn't comparing the same thing. Whether the underlying trend moved at all is genuinely unclear until someone reconciles the two coding schemes.

Benchmark contamination is the quiet crisis in model evaluation. If test items appeared anywhere in the training corpus, the reported score measures memorization, not capability. Most papers don't run decontamination checks, and the ones that do rarely publish the overlap statistics.

Over a thirty-year horizon, low-cost index funds beat the large majority of actively managed funds after fees. This is about as close to settled as finance gets. It is also completely compatible with some individual managers being genuinely skilled. Both things are true.

Self-reported sleep duration correlates only moderately with actigraphy, and the gap isn't random — it's larger among people with insomnia symptoms. So a lot of the sleep-and-health literature is measuring beliefs about sleep alongside sleep itself, in unknown proportion.

That poll is within the margin of error, which means the race is a coin flip and not a lead. Also worth checking the house effect: this pollster has leaned two points in one direction all cycle, which is within normal variation but worth pricing in.

The replication rate for social priming studies came in around a third. That's not a scandal about individual researchers, it's a structural result of small samples, flexible analysis, and journals that only publish positive findings. Fix the incentives and the rate moves.

The trial hit its surrogate endpoint, not a clinical one. Tumor shrinkage is not the same as survival, and the correlation between the two varies enormously by cancer type. Sometimes the surrogate predicts well. Often it doesn't. Read which one was measured.

Grid reliability with high renewable penetration is a storage and transmission problem, not an impossibility. The costs are real and the engineering is hard. Both the people saying it's trivial and the people saying it's physically impossible are overstating their case considerably.

Early-childhood test score gains often fade by third grade, but the same programs show effects on high school completion and earnings decades later. That's a weird pattern and nobody fully explains it. It does suggest test scores are a poor proxy for whatever is actually happening.

The minimum wage literature genuinely disagrees with itself, and that's fine. Different identification strategies, different labor markets, different magnitudes of increase. Anyone who tells you the evidence is unanimous in either direction has read one paper and stopped.

Antibiotic resistance is a rate problem, not a threshold problem. Every unnecessary prescription nudges selection pressure a little. No individual prescription is the catastrophe, which is exactly why stewardship is hard to enforce at the level of a single patient visit.

Disengagement-per-mile is a bad autonomy metric. It's self-reported, definitions vary between companies, and it rewards operating in easy conditions. Comparing two firms on this number tells you mostly about their testing routes and internal reporting culture.

Streaming platforms release viewership numbers selectively and define a view differently from each other and from themselves last year. Any ranking assembled from those disclosures is closer to a press strategy artifact than an audience measurement.

The protein RDA is a floor for preventing deficiency, not an optimum for building muscle. But the curve flattens sooner than fitness marketing implies, and above roughly 1.6 grams per kilogram the marginal returns in the trial data get very hard to detect.

Attribution science can say a heat wave became several times more likely in a warmed climate. It generally can't say the event was caused by warming in the way people mean when they say caused. That distinction survives the press cycle about half the time.

Went through the city budget line by line. The item everyone is angry about is 0.4 percent of general fund spending. The items nobody is discussing are pensions and debt service, which together are roughly a third. Outrage allocation is not tracking dollar allocation.

Microbiome research is genuinely exciting and also about six years away from most of the claims being made for it. Correlations between gut composition and basically every condition exist. Causal direction is established for very few, and personalized interventions have a thin evidence base.

If a protocol offers twenty percent yield, the first question is where the yield comes from. Sometimes it's real fee revenue. More often it's token emissions, which is a transfer from future holders to current ones dressed up as a return. Ask which.

Two air quality monitors four miles apart in the same city can report meaningfully different readings, and siting explains much of the gap — height, proximity to roadways, local terrain. Neighborhood-level claims from a single sensor deserve more skepticism than they get.

Survey response rates have fallen below ten percent for most phone polling. Weighting fixes what you can observe and model. It cannot fix a systematic difference between people who answer unknown numbers and people who don't, if that difference correlates with the thing you're measuring.

GDP growth and median household income can move in opposite directions for years at a stretch, and often have. Neither statistic is lying. They're measuring different things, and which one you cite usually reveals what you already believed before you looked.

Total volume of high-level nuclear waste produced in this country since the 1950s would fit on a single football field stacked a few meters deep. That's a real fact and it still doesn't resolve the siting problem, which is political and intergenerational rather than volumetric.

Radiocarbon dates come with error bars that most popular coverage drops entirely. A date reported as 3,200 years old might carry a range of a couple of centuries at two sigma. Whole narratives about which civilization influenced which get built inside that uncertainty.

Designing a hallucination eval is harder than it looks. You need questions with verifiable answers, distractors that are plausible, and a scoring rubric that distinguishes a confident wrong answer from an appropriate refusal. Most published evals conflate the last two.

Before-and-after studies of bike infrastructure have an obvious selection problem: cities build lanes on streets where crashes already happened, so regression to the mean inflates the apparent benefit. The better studies use comparison corridors, and they still find a benefit, just a smaller one.

Observational data made vitamin D look protective for nearly everything. The randomized trials have been mostly null outside of correcting genuine deficiency. The likeliest explanation is reverse causation: being sick and indoors lowers your levels rather than the other way around.

The per-stream payout figure everyone quotes isn't a rate that exists anywhere. Royalties are a pool divided pro rata, so an artist's payout depends on total platform streams that month. Which means the number changes even if your listeners don't.

Acres burned is a poor standalone measure of fire severity. Fuel load, canopy mortality, and soil effects vary enormously across the same acreage. A large low-intensity burn can be ecologically beneficial. The headline number treats both cases identically.

A risk score can be well calibrated across groups and still produce different false positive rates across those groups, if base rates differ. This isn't a bug someone forgot to fix, it's a mathematical impossibility result. Which fairness criterion you pick is a value judgment.

Most remote work productivity studies measure output in the one or two domains that are easy to count — tickets closed, calls handled, lines committed. Mentorship, tacit knowledge transfer, and the slow decay of institutional memory don't show up for several years.

The inflation number you feel and the inflation number that gets published differ mainly in basket composition. If your spending is concentrated in rent, childcare, and insurance, your personal rate has been well above headline for a while. The index isn't wrong, it's just not about you.

The meta-analysis on adolescent social media and wellbeing lands on an association roughly the size of the association with wearing glasses. That's the honest finding. It's compatible with real harm to a vulnerable subgroup being averaged away, which is the part worth studying next.

Readmission penalties reduced readmissions and also increased observation-status stays that don't count as admissions. Some of the improvement is real, some is reclassification, and the literature has spent a decade arguing about the ratio without converging.

Doping test sensitivity has improved faster than public understanding of what a negative result means. A clean test means nothing above the detection threshold for the substances screened, at the time sampled. That's a much narrower claim than innocence.

If you test enough splits — home/away, day/night, count, handedness, month — something clears the significance bar by chance. Sports analytics runs on enormous search spaces and mostly doesn't correct for them. Treat any surprising split as a hypothesis, not a finding.

Desalination cost per acre-foot has fallen substantially and is still several times the cost of conservation or reuse in most basins. It's a reasonable marginal supply for coastal cities with no cheaper option. It is not a general solution to water scarcity, especially inland.

The lead exposure cohort studies are among the more convincing natural experiments in public health, because the phase-out timing varied across regions in ways unrelated to local outcomes. Even so, the effect size attributed to lead in the strongest papers remains contested.

A risk-limiting audit is a statistical procedure with a stated confidence level, not a full recount. It's good practice and it's designed to catch outcome-changing error, not every individual discrepancy. People on both sides routinely describe the results as proving more than they can.

Semiconductor lead times are a useful leading indicator and a terrible coincident one. Orders get double-booked during shortages and cancelled in gluts, so the series overshoots in both directions. The amplitude of the swing is largely an artifact of ordering behavior.

Some reefs recover from bleaching within a decade and some don't, and the variance between sites is larger than the variance between years. Local water quality and herbivore populations explain a good deal of it. Averaging across sites throws away the actionable information.

Sodium restriction trials show clear benefit at very high intake and get genuinely murky in the middle range. There's a plausible J-curve, the evidence for it is not strong, and the guideline number reflects a policy judgment under uncertainty rather than a demonstrated optimum.

Venture returns are power law distributed, which means median fund performance tells you almost nothing and the mean is driven by a handful of outcomes. Reported IRRs before exits are marks, not money. Both facts are widely known and routinely ignored in fundraising decks.

Historical literacy rates are mostly reconstructed from signature counts on legal documents, which measures something narrower than literacy and oversamples people who had reason to sign documents. The long-run trend is probably right. The levels in any given decade are soft.

Exoplanet detection methods are biased toward large planets in short orbits, because that's what transit and radial velocity find most easily. So the observed population is not the actual population, and every claim about how common Earth-like planets are carries a correction step you should ask about.

Antidepressants beat placebo in trials by a margin that's statistically solid and clinically modest on average. Averages hide responders and non-responders. The honest framing is that they work well for some people, not at all for others, and we can't yet predict which in advance.

Farebox recovery ratio is a bad primary metric for transit because the point of the system is the economic activity it enables, not its own revenue. Roads aren't held to this standard. That said, low recovery does create a real fiscal fragility worth planning around.

Half the A/B tests I see are underpowered to detect the effect size the team is hoping for, which means a null result is uninformative and a positive result is probably inflated. Run the power calculation before the test, not after the result disappoints you.

Correlation isn't causation, but a well-designed natural experiment can get you most of the way there. The question to ask isn't whether it's observational, it's whether the assignment mechanism is plausibly as-good-as-random conditional on what's controlled for.

The hard question for any carbon offset is additionality: would the tree have stood, or the methane been captured, without the payment? It is very difficult to verify a counterfactual, which is why offset quality varies from genuinely good to essentially fictional.

Firearm policy effects vary enormously by state context, baseline enforcement, and which outcome you measure. Studies that pool across all states produce averages that describe nowhere in particular. This is a place where the heterogeneity is the finding, not noise around one.

Teacher value-added scores are noisy enough that a teacher's ranking can swing a couple of deciles between years with no change in practice. Useful in aggregate for research. Genuinely poor as an individual high-stakes evaluation instrument, which is mostly how they get used.

Reported recycling rates typically count material collected, not material actually reprocessed into new goods. For most plastic resins the gap between those two numbers is enormous. This isn't a reason to stop sorting; it's a reason to be skeptical of the headline percentage.

Forecasts of AI-driven job displacement span an order of magnitude across credible studies, because they differ on task decomposition, adoption speed, and whether new roles are counted. The honest summary is wide uncertainty, which nobody gets invited on television to say.

The point-in-time count undercounts homelessness, especially people doubled up or in vehicles, and the size of the undercount varies by jurisdiction and weather on the night of the count. Year-over-year changes in the count partly measure changes in counting effort.

The house edge on parlays is far larger than on single bets, and the product is designed so the correlated-looking legs feel more likely than the math implies. You can enjoy betting and still know that the expected value is negative by construction.

For a symptom with a one-in-fifty-thousand serious cause, a test with ninety-nine percent specificity still generates far more false positives than true ones. Diagnostic reasoning is mostly base rates, and base rates are the part that intuition handles worst.

Peer review catches some errors and misses many. It was never designed as a fraud detector and it's bad at being one. Treating publication as a certification of truth rather than as a weak filter explains a lot of downstream public confusion about science.

The seed oil argument rests mostly on mechanistic reasoning about omega-6 ratios plus some observational work. The randomized evidence on replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat points the other way. Mechanism is a hypothesis generator, not evidence of outcomes.

Endowment spending rules are typically a smoothed percentage of a trailing average, which is why a great market year doesn't produce an immediate budget windfall. Also most of the fund is restricted to specific donor purposes and legally can't be moved to whatever is currently urgent.

Surveillance for novel influenza is sparse enough that the absence of detected human cases is weak evidence about actual human cases. This cuts in both directions. It's a reason for humility about reassuring statements and about alarming ones alike.

Speed test results depend on server selection, time of day, and whether your router or your device is the bottleneck. A single test tells you about one path at one moment. Sustained throughput during peak hours is the number that actually describes your service.

Prescribing volume fell substantially while overdose deaths kept climbing, because the mortality driver shifted to illicit supply. Both facts are in the same datasets. Policy arguments that cite one and omit the other are describing a different epidemic than the one happening.

Stable isotope analysis of ancient remains gives you broad dietary categories — marine versus terrestrial protein, roughly what kind of plants — not menus. The reconstructions in museum placards are considerably more specific than the underlying chemistry supports.

My honest estimate on fault-tolerant quantum computing is wide: plausibly a decade, plausibly considerably longer, with meaningful probability that a materials problem we haven't hit yet stretches it further. Anyone giving you a tight range is forecasting their funding needs.

Average wage growth can rise purely because low-wage jobs disappeared from the sample. That's composition effect, not raises. During any period of sharp employment change you want to look at wage growth for continuously employed workers instead of the headline average.

Color in restored films is a judgment call, not a recovery of ground truth. Original negatives have faded unevenly, reference prints disagree with each other, and the people who saw the theatrical release are mostly gone. Every restoration is an argument about intent.

A model scoring well on long-context retrieval benchmarks often degrades sharply on tasks requiring synthesis across the same context. Finding a needle is not the same as reasoning over the haystack, and the benchmarks that get quoted mostly measure the former.

Nameplate capacity for wind means output at the rated wind speed, which is not most hours. Capacity factor is the number that matters, and it varies from the low twenties to over fifty percent depending on siting and turbine class. Comparing nameplate to a gas plant's output is a category error.

Nearly every screen time and child outcome association shrinks when you control for household income, parental education, and neighborhood. What remains is small and inconsistent across measurement approaches. The within-family designs are the ones worth reading here.

Check the disclosure section before the recommendation section. A guideline panel where most voting members have industry relationships isn't automatically wrong, but it changes how much independent verification a reader should want before adopting the recommendation.

Predictive policing creates a feedback loop: you send patrols where you've previously recorded incidents, which generates more recorded incidents there, which the model reads as confirmation. The model can be technically accurate about its own training distribution and still be useless.

Cost per QALY is an uncomfortable metric and every alternative is worse. Refusing to price health outcomes doesn't avoid rationing, it just moves the rationing somewhere less visible and less accountable. The arguments worth having are about the threshold and the weights.

An I-squared above seventy-five means the studies in your meta-analysis are measuring meaningfully different things, and pooling them produces an average of incomparable quantities. The forest plot is more informative than the diamond at the bottom in that situation.

Microplastic counts across studies aren't comparable because detection limits differ by an order of magnitude between methods. Some labs count particles down to a micron, some stop at fifty. Rising reported concentrations partly reflect improving instruments.

Fertility decline shows up across countries with wildly different housing costs, childcare policies, and religious composition, which is a problem for every single-cause explanation on offer. Whatever is driving it appears to be something that generalizes across those differences.

Flood insurance pricing was historically based on maps that lagged development and ignored rainfall-driven flooding away from rivers. Updating to catastrophe models produces enormous premium changes that are actuarially defensible and politically impossible. Both of those are true at once.

The three-point revolution was straightforward expected value arithmetic that took the league roughly fifteen years to fully act on. The interesting question isn't why it happened, it's why the adjustment lagged the analysis for so long once the math was public.

Supplements are regulated as food, not drugs, which means no premarket efficacy review and inconsistent verification that the label matches the contents. Third-party testing programs help. The baseline assumption for an unverified product should be that potency varies batch to batch.

Urban heat island measurement depends enormously on sensor placement — a monitor over asphalt in full sun and one in a shaded park a block away can differ by several degrees. City-to-city comparisons often compare station networks more than they compare cities.

Large parts of the security-critical open source stack are maintained by a handful of unpaid people. This is a known structural risk that gets attention for about two weeks after each major incident and then stops being anyone's budget line.

CPI and the GDP deflator diverge because they cover different baskets and handle substitution differently. Neither is the true inflation rate, because there isn't one. Pick the index that matches the decision you're making and say which one you picked.

Food frequency questionnaires ask people to recall average consumption over a year. Recall is bad, portion estimation is worse, and the errors correlate with body weight and health consciousness. This is the measurement instrument underneath a substantial share of nutrition headlines.

The legal standard is whether the prosecution met its burden, not whether the defendant did it. Those come apart regularly, and public commentary collapses them constantly. An acquittal is a statement about evidence sufficiency, which is narrower than most reporting implies.

Earthquake early warning gives you seconds to tens of seconds, derived from the gap between P and S wave arrival. That's enough to stop a train or halt surgery. It is not prediction, and the systems get oversold as prediction in nearly every news segment about them.

Chart methodology has changed repeatedly — streaming ratios, bundle rules, how sales windows are counted. Comparing a number one run from this decade to one from three decades ago is comparing outputs of two different formulas, not two levels of popularity.

The teacher shortage is severe in specific subjects and specific regions and doesn't exist in others. National vacancy figures average a rural physics crisis with an urban elementary surplus, producing a number that describes no district's actual staffing situation.

Cultivated meat cost curves have fallen steeply from an absurd starting point, which is the easy part of any learning curve. The unresolved questions are bioreactor scale-up, growth media cost, and whether the process economics work outside pilot volumes.

Heat wave mortality studies have to account for displacement — some deaths would have occurred within weeks regardless, so excess deaths during the event are partly offset by a deficit afterward. The net figure is smaller than the peak figure and more honest.

Surveys of academic economists find near-consensus on some questions — trade gains, carbon pricing, rent control effects — and wide dispersion on others. Public discourse tends to sample from the dispersed set and conclude the field agrees on nothing.

Real-world EV battery degradation data from large fleets has come in better than early lab projections, with most packs retaining the large majority of capacity past a hundred thousand miles. Fast-charging frequency and climate explain most of the variance between vehicles.

A patent cliff shifts revenue from the originator to generics and lowers prices, which is the system working as designed. The argument worth having is about exclusivity length and evergreening tactics, not about whether generic entry should happen at all.

Citizen science data quality is usually fine for presence and terrible for absence, because volunteers don't record nothing. Occupancy models that account for detection probability handle this. Raw counts from observation platforms usually don't, and get cited anyway.

A useful habit: before sharing something that confirms what you already thought, spend thirty seconds looking for the strongest version of the opposing case. Most of the time it's weaker than you feared. Occasionally it isn't, and those are the valuable occasions.
